1:
Clarke begins with the verb. To sanctify signifies to consecrate, separate and set a person apart from all secular purposes to some religious use; and it answers, he says, to the Greek word for holy, which he derives from a privative and the word for earth — everything consecrated to God being separated from earthly uses, so that a saint is by etymology a person separated from the earth. What the claim rests on is disputed: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the right to the firstborn was founded on Jehovah's being Lord and Creator of all things, so that every created object, owing its life to him, should have its life devoted to him: that is what Kurtz maintains, and maintains without scriptural proof. The ground stated expressly elsewhere is historical rather than metaphysical: on the day when Jehovah smote all the firstborn of Egypt, he sanctified these to himself. Ellicott reads the demand as simple equity on that footing — it was reasonable that the firstborn of Israel, spared when the Egyptian firstborn were destroyed, should thenceforth be regarded as his, and reasonable too that the demand should extend to the beasts, since they had been spared as well. The requirement that all future firstborn should also be his was meant, he adds, to perpetuate the memory of the deliverance and fix it in the mind of the nation.

Henry turns the claim into an argument about affection. The parents were not to regard themselves as having any interest in their firstborn until they had solemnly presented them to God, recognised his title, and received them back from him again — and Wesley repeats that almost word for word. From it Henry draws three rules: that whatever is spared to us by a special distinguishing mercy should be dedicated to God's honour; that God, who is the first and best, should have the first and best; and that since the firstborn were the joy and hope of their families, it appears we love God best when we are willing to part with what we love best in this world. Calvin calls the offering a mark of separation between Israel and the heathen, and extends its reach: though God commands only the firstborn of Abraham's race to be offered, this must be carried out to the sanctification of the whole people, since in saying the firstborn were his because they especially owed their preservation to his mercy, he signifies for the same reason that all were his own.

The mechanics were exact. Gill notes that the Targum of Jonathan limits the law to males, females being neither sacrificed nor redeemed; of clean creatures the firstborn were sacrificed and of unclean redeemed with a price, and the firstborn of men were redeemed too, because it was not lawful to sacrifice them, the money going to the priests and so to God. Clarke adds the finer rules — the first male was not offered if a female had been born before him, and where a man had several wives the firstborn of each was offered if a male; and he sets beside the law a comparison from Ward's account of Hindoo custom, where the firstborn of a goat or a man is vowed to an idol. Calvin explains the phrase about opening the womb as the beginning of generation, and takes the words among the children of Israel, applied to beasts as well as offspring, as distinguishing the wild animals from the tame and domestic. Ellicott follows the ordinance forward: redemption was substituted for unclean beasts because they could not be sacrificed, and the redemption of firstborn sons followed once the Levitical priesthood was established and their own services were no longer needed — an ordinance the Jews still observe for children, redeeming the son who has opened the womb on the thirtieth day after birth.
3:
Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting: the directions for the seven days of unleavened bread were made known to the people on the very day of the exodus, at the first station, Succoth, and what stands here repeats only the most important points while enjoining the yearly commemoration. Calvin asks why anything should be repeated at all, and answers that the purpose is not instruction but stimulus. Moses had already expressed the matter with so much clearness that no further explanation was needed; the repetition was useful to rouse them, so that they might give themselves to the duty with greater zeal, and especially lest after a longer lapse of time their ardour should, as usually happens, gradually abate. Calvin also draws the two commands of the chapter together, observing that the sanctifying of the firstborn and the keeping of the passover have one and the same object — that their deliverance should hold the elect people to the special service of the true God. Keil and Delitzsch add two notes on the wording: Egypt is here called a slave-house, because Israel was put to slave-labour there and treated as a slave population, and the phrase rendered strength of hand is more emphatic than the commoner expression it replaces.

Ellicott counts the means by which the memory was to be secured, and finds four working together. The month was made to begin the ecclesiastical year; the Passover was instituted; the seven days of unleavened bread were appointed; and the redemption of the firstborn was commanded, with the questions from children that it would inevitably provoke. On the month itself he explains the name: Abib means green ears of corn, or simply greenness, and the month so called was the one in which the wheat came into ear and the earth generally renewed its verdure. It was a shifting month rather than a fixed one, properly beginning with the day of the full moon next after the vernal equinox, and it kept that name until the Babylonian captivity, when the Babylonian name Nisan displaced it. Gill dates the departure itself to the fifteenth of that month, on the authority of the Targum of Jonathan.

Calvin reads the promise of the land as doing two opposite kinds of work at once. First he notes the scale of what is being commanded: Moses compares the single day of their coming out with the whole time of their sojourning in Canaan, as if to say that they were redeemed not for a transient joy but to be mindful of the blessing throughout all ages. Then he asks why the extent and fertility of the country should be praised again here, and gives two reasons. The first is precautionary — lest after such glorious victories pride should possess their minds, and in the abundance of their good things their eyes should be closed by fatness. The second is the opposite: that by the very multitude of their possessions they might be the more incited to gratitude and to the service of God. Conquerors of so many nations, lords of so rich and extensive a territory, might well wax wanton and grow less devoted, unless they were reminded that they owed to God alone both the conquest and the dominion. Which is why the names of the dispossessed nations are recited and the land called one flowing with milk and honey: in proportion to God's goodness toward them, Calvin says, they would be the more inexcusable if they did not earnestly labour to testify their gratitude.
5:
The conditional opening — when the LORD shall bring thee into the land — carries a legal consequence that three of the witnesses draw independently. Clarke thinks it pretty evident from this that the Israelites were not obliged to celebrate the Passover, or keep the feast of unleavened bread, until they had been brought into the promised land; Wesley says the same, that till then they were not bound to keep it without a particular command from God. Ellicott reports Kalisch reaching that conclusion from this verse and one in the previous chapter, and supplies the historical test: on that view only two Passovers were kept before the entry — one by Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, one by Joshua at Gilgal. Ellicott also notes that the full number of the Canaanitish peoples was seven, of which five are named here, the omitted Perizzites and Girgashites seeming the least important; the most important were the Canaanites, Hittites and Amorites, which is why those three are almost always placed first — though at the exodus, and for centuries after, the most powerful appear to have been the Hittites.

Gill sets himself against the received interpretation on what the seven days require. The Jews gather from this place, he says, that the obligation to eat unleavened bread lasted no longer than the first night, and that for the remaining days it was enough to abstain from leaven while eating what they pleased. Gill will not have it: the words are very express, here and in the next verse alike, for eating the unleavened bread as well as abstaining from the leavened — and he adds a reason from the purpose of the rite, since otherwise it would not be so plain a commemoration of the circumstances they were in when they came out of Egypt, this bread of affliction being precisely what would put them in mind of them. He dates the period from the evening of the fourteenth to that of the twenty-first, and notes on Leo Modena's authority that the cakes of eggs and sugar the Jews now use are for the dainty and the sick, who eat unleavened bread as well. Ellicott observes that the seventh day carried a holy convocation, and that the Jews regard that day as the anniversary of the passage of the Red Sea.

Wesley describes how thoroughly the leaven was put away: before the feast the Jews cast all leavened bread out of their houses, burning it, burying it, or breaking it small and throwing it to the wind, and searched with lighted candles in every corner. He gives the strictness two purposes — to make the feast more solemn and therefore the more noticed by the children, who would ask why so much ado was made; and to teach how solicitous we should be to put away from us all sin. On the instruction that follows, Calvin marks a change from the previous chapter. There the words were when your children shall say unto you; here God commands more briefly that his goodness be proclaimed although nobody asks about it, because parents ought to be voluntarily disposed to educate their children in the fear of God. Gill finds the rabbis at the same point, reporting from Maimonides that the telling is owed to all the children, sons and daughters, and owed even unasked, and from Jarchi that it is meant for a son who does not know how to ask. Calvin adds why the observance had to be annual — the memory should be renewed each year lest it fade, since religion is easily neglected unless men are diligently exercised in its study — and explains the closing figure: their redemption was to be set before their eyes in the passover, as a ring upon the finger or an ornament bound upon the forehead is constantly in sight.
9:
Whether the sign on the hand is a figure or an instruction divides the bench. Gill takes it as figure, and adds a reason that cuts at the practice built on it. These are not God's words or Moses' but an Israelite parent's to his son, telling him the feast of unleavened bread would refresh his memory of what God did for his people, just as tying a thing on the hand or setting it before the eye brings something to remembrance. The Jews understand it literally, Gill grants, and the use of phylacteries follows — but such a practice, he objects, could be of no use to answer the end the verse itself goes on to name, that the law of the LORD should be in the mouth. Wesley disposes of it in a line, calling the expressions proverbial and taking them to denote things which are never out of our thoughts. Keil and Delitzsch stand between. The words presuppose a real custom of wearing mnemonic signs on hand and forehead, so that the sign probably consisted of a bracelet round the wrist and the memorial of a band worn on the brow; but they insist the allusion is not to the heathen practice of branding soldiers and slaves with marks, since the parallel commands to bind them upon the hand rule out both branding and writing — and the words are then used figuratively, as a proverbial expression giving emphasis to the injunction to bear the precept continually in mind.

Clarke sets out what the literal reading produced, in detail and without comment on its rightness. Four portions of the law were written on slips of parchment or vellum: the command to sanctify the firstborn and the passage that follows it in this chapter, together with two passages from Deuteronomy — thirty verses in all. Those meant for the head were written on four separate slips, each rolled by itself and placed in four compartments joined together in one piece of leather; those for the hand were written on a single piece in four columns and rolled from one end to the other. All had to be correct transcripts of the Mosaic text, without one redundant or deficient letter, or they were not lawful to be worn. The head-pieces were tied so as to rest on the forehead, the others usually on the inside of the left arm a little above the elbow. Ellicott confirms that the Jews themselves trace the practice to the time of the exodus and rest it on this verse.

Ellicott then takes up an objection raised against the whole institution. A similar custom is known to have prevailed in Egypt, and it has been urged from this that Moses cannot have instituted phylacteries, since he would hardly have encouraged an Egyptian superstition. Ellicott answers that the adoption of Egyptian customs, purged of their superstition, is quite in the spirit of the Mosaic institutions and in no way reprehensible: if the Israelites were addicted to wearing amulets as the Egyptians were, it was a wise provision to substitute the solemn words of the Law for the magic charms of sorcerers, and so turn a current superstition to good account — by which the Law was honoured, and the passages chosen came to be widely known to those who wore them. On the following verse Gill enters a correction of his own against the Targum of Jonathan, which takes the ordinance to be kept as the ordinance of the phylacteries: it is the ordinance of unleavened bread that is meant. Keil and Delitzsch fix its season precisely, at the appointed time from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of Abib, and explain the Hebrew idiom rendered from year to year as meaning literally from days to days — that is, as often as those days returned.
11:
Keil and Delitzsch explain that the law briefly stated at the head of the chapter is now given at length, to come into force when Israel had taken possession of the land. The verb rendered set apart means literally to cause to pass over to Jehovah — to consecrate, or give up to him as a sacrifice — and the general expression about all that opens the womb is then particularised in three clauses: the clean domestic cattle, that is oxen, sheep and goats, but only the males; the ass, as the commonest of the unclean domestic animals, standing for the whole of that class; and the firstborn of the children of Israel. The female firstborn, of man and beast alike, were exempted from consecration altogether. Gill takes set apart as the explanation of sanctify, showing that what is meant is separating a creature to the use and service of God, causing it to pass out of a man's own power to be the Lord's only; Ellicott adds the practical sense, that it was separated off from the rest of the herd so as not to be mixed with those not sanctified. On the naming of the Canaanites alone, Ellicott observes that either their importance or their genealogical position caused the term to be used inclusively of all the Palestinian nations.

Calvin ties the ordinance back to its occasion: by it the people were to bear witness to the special blessing which preserved them when God destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians. He notes that the animals were to be brought to God in order to be slain at the tabernacle, it being a common figure of speech to say that the faithful and their gifts were set in God's sight when they entered it. He then offers a conjecture about a related rule, that the firstborn were kept seven days before being offered: this was to prevent deceptions, since if the young had been torn earlier from their dams and delivered at once to the priests the offering would have been useless — though Calvin does not doubt the eighth day was fixed on because it was the day prescribed for circumcision. The exception for the ass he explains simply, that a price was paid because the offering of the animal itself would have been unclean; and children had to be redeemed because they could neither be offered in sacrifice nor made priests.

Henry draws the doctrine out of the two halves of the law. The firstlings of clean beasts, if males, were sacrificed; those of unclean beasts were redeemed with a lamb or else knocked on the head — from which Henry takes his rule, that whatsoever is unclean, as we all are by nature, will be destroyed if it be not redeemed. The firstborn of their children were to be redeemed and by no means sacrificed, as the Gentiles sacrificed theirs to Moloch, the price being afterwards fixed at five shekels; and Henry reads the arrangement forward, that we were all obnoxious to the wrath and curse of God, and are redeemed by the blood of Christ that we may be joined to the church of the firstborn. That children needed redeeming as much as the firstlings of unclean beasts he takes as a comment on their nature — our children are by nature polluted, and who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? He expects the practice itself to prompt the catechising that follows: seeing all the firstlings thus devoted, the children would ask what it meant, and must be told that God's special property in them was founded on his having preserved them from the sword of the destroying angel — and that, being so delivered, they must serve him.
13:
Ellicott begins from what the verse does not say. Nothing is mentioned of the Israelites possessing horses, and for good reason: horses were well known in Egypt but kept only by kings and great men, and the Hebrews had never been in a position to own any. Asses, by contrast, were exceedingly common and formed the ordinary beasts of burden in the country, so that in default of camels, which the Israelites seem not to have owned either, they must have carried their tents and baggage on asses. The animal's uncleanness was pronounced in Egypt too, where the ass is said to have been Typhonian, Set the Evil Principle being represented with long ears which may be an ass's. Clarke reads the case more broadly: since the parallel law speaks of the firstling of an unclean beast generally, the ass here stands for unclean beasts at large. Gill reports the debate from the other side, that Jarchi thought the ass alone was to be redeemed and no other unclean creature, but judges his reasons insufficient — horses, camels, dogs and swine are all included, and the ass is named because there was a greater plenty of them and they were so useful, so that if these were redeemed then much more those of less value. Gill adds, from the ass's prominence in the law, a suggestion that here may lie the origin of the old calumny that the Jews worshipped an ass's head.

Gill cites the Jewish canon that the firstling of an ass might be redeemed with a lamb only — not with a calf, nor a goat or ram, nor a lamb slain or torn to pieces — the lamb being given to the priest. Clarke adds the consequence that made the transaction worth making: the lamb went to the Lord, that is to his priest, and thereafter the owner might put the ass to his own service, which without redemption he could not do. Ellicott points out that the exchange was generous to the owner, since the ass colt must have been of considerably more value than the lamb. The alternative to redemption draws his sharpest comment. There will always be in every nation, he says, those who grudge to make any offering to God and who seek to evade every requisition for a gift; to check such niggardliness this law about breaking the animal's neck was made — and it would be effectual without ever needing to be put in force.

For the children the price was fixed. Wesley says simply that it was settled by the law; Clarke specifies five shekels of the sanctuary, each weighing twenty gerahs, and reports that the Hebrew doctors teach that a son whose father had neglected to redeem him was obliged to redeem himself when he came of age. Ellicott explains the arrangement as anticipating what came later, when the tribe of Levi was taken in lieu of the firstborn for the service of the sanctuary and Israelites of the other tribes were bound to redeem their sons by a payment to the priests. Keil and Delitzsch pause on the phrase describing Pharaoh, which is elliptical in the Hebrew and means that he made hard — his heart being understood — to let them go. On the closing figure Gill takes it as he took the earlier one: these laws will keep their reason, the destruction of Egypt's firstborn and the preservation of Israel's, as fresh in memory as a token tied on the hand, and as plainly discerned as anything on a man's forehead; Wesley agrees that the sense is as conspicuous as something fixed between the eyes. Ellicott makes a distinction worth keeping, however: the injunctions here might undoubtedly be explained as metaphorical, but those in the parallel Deuteronomy passage seem to have been intended, and were certainly understood, literally.
17:
Two roads lay open. Henry describes a short cut from north Egypt to south Canaan, perhaps four or five days' journey, and a much longer way round through the wilderness, which God chose. Ellicott traces the short road — from Tanis along the coast to Pelusium, then to Gaza, Ascalon and Ashdod — reckoning the distance at no more than two hundred miles, which might have been done in a fortnight. He also corrects the clause explaining the refusal: not although that was near but because that was near — God did not lead them that way precisely because it was the near one. Calvin gives the reason plainly: had they met enemies so soon, a ready means of return would have encouraged them back into Egypt, and God was willing to set a barrier behind them in the very difficulty of the journey. Clarke says the same from the other end — had they begun their march with a military campaign, there is little room to doubt they would have been discouraged, rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and returned. Gill notes what made returning tempting: Pharaoh had not merely given them leave but urged them to be gone in haste.

Why they were unfit is answered most sharply by Clarke, and his answer is about what slavery does. Their long servitude had so degraded their minds that they were incapable of any great or noble exertion, and only on the ground of this mental degradation — the infallible consequence of slavery, he calls it — can we account for the dastardly acts and murmurings that fill the rest of the history. Besides, they were probably unarmed and wholly unequipped for battle, encumbered with their flocks and utensils. Calvin describes the same people from within: we know how great was their supineness as soon as any difficulty appeared, and how quick they were to revolt whenever a heavier burden was laid on them; powerless in arms and without experience of tactics, they would not have borne a single assault, but would rather have submitted to the Egyptians with supplications for forgiveness. Ellicott supplies the other half of the mismatch: the Philistines were already strong and warlike, possibly the Purusata of the Egyptian remains; by Joshua's time they held their five fortresses, and under the judges rose to the leading position in the region — Palestine takes its name from them, and would not have done so had they not been a remarkable race.

Henry then gathers the positive reasons. The Egyptians were to be drowned in the Red Sea; Israel was to be humbled and proved in the wilderness; God had given Moses the sign that they should serve him at this mountain; and they had told Pharaoh they must go three days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice, so were bound to bend their march that way or be exclaimed against as notorious dissemblers. Above all, before they engaged their enemies matters had to be settled between them and their God — laws given, ordinances instituted, covenants sealed — for which they had to retire into the solitudes of a wilderness, the only closet, as Henry puts it, for such a crowd. Calvin adds a strategic reason: had they met the Canaanites in war at once, the Egyptians would by no means have let them alone, but aided by so many peoples would have hemmed the Israelites in on every side. Henry closes on the doctrine, setting one scripture against another — he led them about, some hundreds of miles about, and yet he led them forth by the right way. God's way is the right way though it seem about; if we think he does not lead the nearest way, we may be sure he leads the best, and so it will appear at our journey's end. Judge nothing before the time.
18:
The word rendered harnessed is the crux, and Clarke admits it is astonishing what a variety of opinions is entertained about it. His own conclusion is that it refers to the orderly manner in which they began their journey, since to arrange or set in order seems the root idea: where hurry and confusion might have been expected, the writer marks the contrary — otherwise thousands must have been trodden to death. Ellicott is blunter: it is generally agreed that the received translation is wrong. Very few Israelites can have owned armour until after the passage of the Red Sea; nor does the word ever bear the force of harnessed; and though it might mean with their loins girded, that would empty the statement of any point, since loins were always girded for a journey. The best explanation, on Saadia's authority and Gesenius's, is that it means organised, in military order. Calvin works from the root, the word for five, and dismisses two readings before offering his own. That they were furnished with five kinds of arms he calls too absurd; that they were armed under the fifth rib, which the Hebrews almost with one consent maintain, he rejects — whence, he asks, were so many corselets ready to hand? He takes it instead as a word of number, that they went out in ranks of five, since in so great a multitude all advancing at once would have been in one another's way; the Greek rendering, which turns it into the fifth generation, he considers foreign to the narrative.

On Joseph's bones Calvin draws an inference about the whole bondage: the memory of the promised deliverance had never departed from the people, for unless Joseph's adjuration had been currently spoken of Moses could never have known of it. Calvin thinks the remains were so deposited that the people's hope might be kept alive by the daily sight of the coffer holding them — as though the holy man, even after death, uplifted from his tomb a sign of their deliverance. Joseph had his brethren more in view than himself: knowing their apathy and the weakness of their faith, he feared that over a longer lapse of time they would despise the promise, and it was that mistrust which made him bind them by an oath rather than a simple injunction. Whether he alone was carried is disputed. Clarke supposes they brought away the remains of all twelve sons of Jacob, each tribe caring for its own patriarch, and argues from Stephen's speech that the fathers as well as Jacob were carried into Sychem — this being the only opportunity that offered. Gill reports Jarchi holding the same but answers that it does not appear from the text; he is equally short with the rabbinic stories of how the burial place was found, dismissing them as fables not worthy of notice.

The stations are uncertain. Keil and Delitzsch derive Succoth from the word for huts and take it for a shepherd encampment south-east of Rameses, with Etham at the end of the desert, where Egypt ends and the desert of Arabia begins. Ellicott admits both positions can only be conjectured, suggesting Succoth near Tel Dafneh and Etham near the modern Ismailia on the verge of the desert; he twice rejects Brugsch — the identification of Etham with the Egyptian Khetam, since the Hebrew aleph never replaces that strong guttural, and the theory that the Red Sea of Exodus was Lake Serbonis. Gill dates the departure from Succoth to the sixteenth of Nisan. Wesley supplies the image that explains the detour: God is said to bring Israel out of Egypt as the eagle brings up her young, teaching them by degrees to fly — it was convenient they should begin with the Amalekites and be prepared for the wars of Canaan by the difficulties of the wilderness.
21:
Four of the witnesses identify the Lord who went before Israel with Christ. Gill takes him for the Angel of Jehovah's presence — not a created angel but the uncreated one, the Word and Son of God, going before Israel's armies as King and Commander. Clarke claims Paul's authority for the same reading; Wesley calls the pillar the Shechinah, a manifestation of the eternal Word; and Henry says simply that Christ was with the church in the wilderness. Calvin agrees God was truly present but enters a caveat about how the language works. Although the words seem in some measure to shut the Lord up in the cloud, we must observe the sacramental mode of speaking, in which God transfers his name to visible figures — not to fix his essence in them or circumscribe his infinity, but to show that he does not deceitfully expose the signs of his presence, the thing signified being truly conjoined with them. He will not have the sign confused with the substance, and turns on Servetus, who pretended the cloud was itself uncreated, as though it were the Deity of Christ: Calvin calls that a mad and execrable notion.

What the pillar did is described three ways, and on one point they contradict. Clarke doubts whether there was more than one pillar, and suggests that if one, it assumed three appearances for three offices: a column of cloud by day to point the way, a pillar of fire by night to light the camp, and — since something more was needed in that desert than a light and a guide — a shelter for the women, children and infirm exposed to the heat. He adds that they seldom travelled by night. Ellicott says the opposite: they marched some part of each day and some part of each night, an arrangement matching modern practice, designed to get the march done before the sun attained full power. Keil and Delitzsch side with Ellicott, reading the closing phrase to mean that they might march at all hours. Ellicott notices a resemblance: the pillar was at once signal and guide — when it moved the people moved, when it stopped they encamped — much as generals used fire and smoke signals at the head of their armies, God having in effect constituted himself the generalissimo of the host, though the thing itself was miraculous.

Why the guide was needed just here is Wesley's observation. In the first two stages it was enough that God directed Moses, who knew the road; but at the edge of the wilderness they needed a guide, and had a very good one, infinitely wise and kind and faithful. Clarke pushes it further: a guide was necessary even had they gone by the direct road, and much more on a circuitous route they knew nothing of — indeed Moses himself very likely did not know the way or the places of encampment until the pillar halted and marked them. Calvin sees an accommodation: God might have shaded them and lit their way by other means, but that his power might be more manifest he added his visible presence, condescending to their ignorance. Wesley draws the comfort out in a series: they need not fear missing their way who were thus led, nor being lost who were thus directed, nor being benighted who were thus illuminated, nor being robbed who were thus protected. And he applies it — those who make the glory of God their end and his word their rule, his Spirit the guide of their affections and his providence the guide of their affairs, may be confident that the Lord goes before them as truly as he went before Israel, though not so sensibly. Henry gives that thought its instrument: the Bible is a light to our feet, and is to us what the pillar was to the Israelites.
22:
Nothing else in the chapter is disputed at such length as how long the pillar lasted. Clarke reports that neither Jews nor Gentiles are agreed. He thinks it very probable the cloud first visited Israel at Succoth, if it did not accompany them from Rameses, and that it stayed until they reached the Jordan opposite Jericho, after which the ark alone marched at their head; but others hold it went no farther than Mount Hor and never appeared after Aaron's death. Gill and Wesley take the longer view without hesitation — it continued through the wilderness to the borders of Canaan, and when they passed over Jordan the ark went before them instead (Joshua 3:6). Wesley adds that it did not leave them even when they seemed to have less occasion for it, and that it was a cloud the wind could not scatter. Ellicott, comparing Exodus 40:38 and Numbers 9:16, fixes the disappearance more narrowly: probably at Abel-shittim (Numbers 33:49). Keil and Delitzsch state the rule all these answers assume — this sign of the presence of God did not depart from Israel so long as the people continued in the wilderness.

Clarke turns the dispute into a principle, and it is the weightiest thing said on the verse. We may safely assert that while the cloud was indispensably necessary it continued, and when it was not, it was removed; and it is worth remarking that the ark of the covenant became its substitute. While a miracle was necessary a miracle was granted; when it was no longer necessary, the testimony of the Lord deposited in the ark was deemed sufficient by him who cannot err. He carries the rule forward into the gospel dispensation: miracles were necessary at its first promulgation, but once the canon of Scripture was complete, the new covenant ratified by the blood of the Lamb and published by the Holy Spirit, God generally withdrew those outward signs, leaving his word for a continual testimony and sealing it on the souls of believers by the Spirit of truth. He notices too that the heathen poets always wrap their gods in cloud when they appear to men, Homer and Virgil abounding in examples, and asks whether they borrowed the figure — as they borrowed much else in their mythology — from the tradition of Jehovah guiding his people through the desert.

Wesley alone presses the pillar for a spiritual sense, and does it by way of Paul: the children of Israel were baptized unto Moses in this cloud (1 Corinthians 10:2). By coming under it they signified their putting themselves under the conduct and command of Moses. Protection draws allegiance; the cloud was the badge of God's protection, and so became the bond of their allegiance. The timing carries the point for him: they were initiated and admitted under that government just as they were entering upon the wilderness, at the moment when the settled road ended and the guidance had to be total. Nor does the figure close with Israel. What the pillar was to them signifies the special conduct and protection which the church of Christ is under in this world.
